# Could the musician closest to the director's left touch him while seated?

**Short answer: Yes. Almost certainly he could — an outstretched arm, helped by a
small lean forward from the hips, would be enough. He would not have to get up.**

## What the video shows

The clip is a single, locked-off wide shot (1280×720, 156.8 s, no cuts) filmed
from inside the audience of a hall — a sports hall fitted out with a temporary
stage, truss and black drapes; the banners read "Akkordeon Orchester Hof", and
the on-screen title is "Tritsch-Tratsch Polka". After the opening seconds the
camera zooms in slightly and then never moves again.

The director (conductor) is the grey-suited, white-haired man standing at centre
frame with his back to the camera, at roughly x ≈ 620 px in the frame. He is
working from his own conductor's desk, which is visible as the horizontal bar
with a central post immediately in front of him (top edge at y ≈ 434 px, about
0.65 m wide). The players sit in a shallow arc around him, nearly all of them
with accordions, each behind a music stand.

Because the director faces away from the camera, "his left" and "screen left"
are opposite sides. I checked both, and the conclusion is the same either way:

* **Screen-left of him** (the reading most people mean when describing a shot)
  sits the player whose head occupies x ≈ 539–582 px, head-top at y ≈ 380 px —
  the light-haired player just beyond his right shoulder. This is the closest
  musician to him anywhere in the picture.
* **On his own left** (screen right) the nearest player's head is at
  x ≈ 682–706 px, an essentially symmetric position, only slightly farther away.

## How close is that player?

The footage is soft and low-contrast, so I measured on temporally averaged
frames (20–50 frames stacked) at 8–12× magnification with a pixel grid overlay,
and calibrated with the director's own body:

* His head measures 41 px across and his shoulders 84 px. Taking a head of about
  0.20 m and a bideltoid shoulder breadth of about 0.48 m, the image scale at his
  distance is roughly 175–200 px per metre. His hips measure 67 px, which matches
  the same scale, so the calibration is self-consistent.
* The lateral gap between his body centre-line (x ≈ 620) and the nearest
  left-hand player's head centre (x ≈ 560) is about 60 px, i.e. only about
  **0.3–0.4 m sideways** — less than one of his own shoulder-widths. His body
  edge and that player's head are practically adjacent in the frame.
* Depth is the part that image position alone cannot show, so I used apparent
  size. That player's head measures about 36–43 px against the director's 41 px.
  Since he is an adult with a bigger head than a teenage player, near-equal
  apparent sizes mean they are at very nearly the same distance from the camera.
  Even on the most pessimistic reading of the blur, the player cannot be more
  than roughly 1.5 m further back; the central estimate is a gap of well under
  1 m. (Occlusion confirms the ordering: the director's body and desk cut across
  the white sheet music on that player's stand, so he is the nearer of the two,
  standing just downstage of the front desks — not several metres in front of
  them.)

Combining the two components, the straight-line distance from the seated
player's torso to the director's body is about **1 m, with a plausible range of
roughly 0.6–1.5 m**.

A corroborating observation: whenever the director sweeps his right hand out to
that side (e.g. at t ≈ 60 s his hand sits at x ≈ 532–552 px, y ≈ 348–367 px), it
passes directly above that player's head — and that is with his elbow still
bent, not at full extension. The two are inside each other's arm-swing space.

## Why that means "yes"

A seated adult's shoulder-to-fingertip reach is about 0.75 m; a seated person who
also leans forward from the hips, without lifting off the chair, can put a
fingertip roughly 1.0–1.2 m from their seated torso. The player's near shoulder
already lies perhaps 0.2 m toward the director, and the director's nearest body
surface (hip/arm) is about 0.2 m inboard of his centre-line, so the actual gap
the hand has to bridge is more like 0.6–0.8 m.

That is comfortably inside a seated reach. The nearest musician to the director
could touch him — most likely with a straightforward extension of the arm, at
worst with a modest lean — without standing up.

## Caveats

* The source video is blurry, dark and heavily compressed, and the conductor
  himself drifts sideways by up to about 0.25 m during the performance, so these
  figures are estimates with maybe ±0.5 m of uncertainty on the separation. The
  qualitative finding is robust, though: he is standing within the arc of
  players, roughly shoulder-to-shoulder with the nearest ones, not out in front
  of them.
* The only real obstruction is furniture, not distance. The player's own music
  stand is in front of him, and the left end of the director's desk sits between
  them, so the reach would be over or around a stand rather than through clear
  air. Neither prevents contact.
* The question assumes that musician is male; at this resolution the player's
  appearance is not clear enough for me to confirm that, which does not change
  the geometry.
